items.title: John Levy — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Lawrence Brown was on trombone. Your key men, like the top trombone player.

ctx.x: Was there something – you said that he’s not going to pay that to a sideman. Was there something lesser about a sideman?

Most of the bands, members of the rhythm section – except the pianist, who in most cases was the leader – got less money than the soloists, than, say, like Johnny Hodges was – I think was the highest paid in the alto section. Then came Carney – Harry Carney. Everybody else made less money than these top soloists. These were the main soloists. Lawrence Brown was on trombone. Your key men, like the top trombone player. The trumpet player at the time – Cootie Williams. They had special solos they had recorded. They…
One of your early recordings was as bass – playing bass with Erroll Garner. Do you recall that? I guess it was his first recording as a leader?

items.title: 52986_Lawrence Brown oral history interview
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] Well, John Levy told me that's an old theatrical superstition.

ctx.x: Where did all these things come about?
Well, John Levy told me that's an old theatrical superstition. The first time I ever heard it was from Duke when a friend of his gave him a pair of slippers.
